common_name: Christmas Carol Hellebore (Fragrant White Christmas Rose)

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained shade; Christmas Carol is a Helleborus niger selection bred for exceptionally early, long-lasting bloom and a light, sweet fragrance unusual among hellebores, often flowering by the actual Christmas holiday in mild climates.

directions: Plant with the crown at soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun. Christmas Carol is a Helleborus niger (Christmas rose) cultivar bred for an especially heavy bud count, extra-long bloom season, and a light, pleasant fragrance rare among hellebores, most of which have little to no scent. Pure white, saucer-shaped flowers with a central boss of golden stamens open from late fall into winter and often continue into early spring, aging to a soft pink blush as they mature, held above dark, leathery, evergreen foliage. Like other Christmas roses, it is more particular about drainage and consistent moisture than the tougher Lenten rose (H. x hybridus) and appreciates a spot that doesn't dry out or stay soggy. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to show off the flowers and reduce leaf spot disease, and top-dress annually with compost, since hellebores are heavy feeders that reward rich soil with a bigger bloom display.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Spotty Dotty is a hybrid mayapple selection prized for enormous, deeply lobed leaves boldly splashed with chocolate-maroon spots, providing dramatic textural impact in the shade garden well beyond its brief spring bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sited where its bold foliage has room to spread. Spotty Dotty is a hybrid Podophyllum selection, likely involving the Chinese species P. delavayi, bred for enormous, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves heavily marbled and spotted with chocolate-maroon blotches over rich green, a striking effect that makes it one of the boldest textural statements available for a shaded border. In spring, dark maroon-red, nodding, cup-shaped flowers appear beneath the emerging foliage, followed later by red fruit, though the flowers are often hidden by the leaves and the foliage display is the plant's main draw. Unlike the common native mayapple (Podophyllum peltatum), which spreads by rhizome and goes dormant by midsummer, Spotty Dotty forms a slowly expanding clump and holds its dramatic foliage well into fall in consistently moist soil. Mulch with leaf litter or compost each fall to mimic its native woodland habitat, and avoid letting the soil dry out during the growing season, since drought causes the large leaves to scorch.

common_name: Dwarf Solomon's Seal (Low Spreading Woodland Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before growth begins or in early fall; unlike the tall, arching native Solomon's seal, Polygonatum humile is a low, spreading Asian species that stays under a foot tall and forms a dense, running groundcover in shade, spreading more vigorously by rhizome than most Solomon's seal species.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; mulch annually with leaf mold or compost. Polygonatum humile is a dwarf Solomon's seal native to woodlands of Japan, Korea, and China, valued in shade gardens for a habit completely different from the taller, arching native species — it stays a low 6-10 inches and spreads steadily by rhizome to form a dense, running groundcover rather than an upright clump, making it useful for carpeting shaded areas under trees and shrubs where taller Solomon's seals would look out of scale. Paired, nodding, small white bell flowers dangle beneath narrow, glossy, parallel-veined leaves in mid-spring, followed by small blue-black berries in fall. Because it spreads more assertively than the clump-forming native species, give it room to run or use it in a contained bed where its groundcover habit is an asset rather than a management problem. It dies back cleanly to the ground each fall and re-emerges reliably each spring, tolerating the dry shade under established trees better than many woodland groundcovers once established.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Polygonatum humile

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun; Desdemona is a classic Ligularia dentata cultivar prized for large, rounded leaves that are deep purple-bronze on top and vivid mahogany-red underneath, though like all ligularias it struggles in zone 9 heat and performs best in cooler climates with consistently moist soil.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun and heat. Desdemona is one of the most widely grown Ligularia dentata cultivars, valued for large, rounded, kidney-shaped leaves that emerge deep bronze-purple and hold rich purple-green coloring on top through the season, with a dramatic mahogany-red underside visible when leaves catch the light or wind. In mid-to-late summer, tall stems carry clusters of bright orange-yellow daisy flowers well above the bold foliage. Like all ligularias, Desdemona wilts dramatically during midday heat, looking severely stressed on hot afternoons before recovering fully overnight — normal behavior for the genus rather than a sign of disease, though it signals the plant wants cooler conditions, consistent moisture, and protection from afternoon sun. It performs best in climates with mild summers and struggles considerably in zone 9 heat and humidity, where siting it in the coolest, most sheltered, consistently moist spot available and mulching heavily to keep roots cool gives it the best chance of success. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ligularia dentata 'Desdemona'

common_name: Jack of Diamonds Brunnera (Large Silver-Splashed Heartleaf Brunnera)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack of Diamonds is a sport of Jack Frost with even larger leaves and bolder silver coloring, and like other named Brunnera cultivars must be propagated from divisions rather than seed to keep the pattern true.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Jack of Diamonds arose as a sport of the celebrated Jack Frost brunnera and is distinguished by noticeably larger leaves and an even bolder, more extensive silver overlay across the heart-shaped foliage, with only fine green veining showing through. In spring, sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage on wiry stems, adding a soft blue counterpoint to the metallic silver leaves. Its large-scale foliage makes a bigger textural and visual statement in the shade border than Jack Frost, useful as a focal point or in bolder plantings alongside hostas and ferns. Consistent moisture is essential — brunnera foliage scorches quickly in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, and in zone 8 gardens it needs reliable afternoon shade and regular watering to look its best through summer. Divide clumps in early spring or late summer when they become crowded, since named cultivars do not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively.
